messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The incident that changed Meera’s life happened on a rainy Thursday in the late 1990s, when she was still a bright-eyed interior‑designer apprentice in her mid‑fifties. She had been called to a small apartment on the south side of the city to assess a kitchen that the landlord said had “gone a little haywire” after a burglary. As she examined the space, a burly police officer arrived, gun drawn, his uniform a stark blue that seemed to swallow the light. He seized her by the wrist, thrust her to the floor, and shouted accusations that had nothing to do with her work. The shock of his grip, the texture of the officer’s gloves on her skin, the sudden weight of his authority—these images were seared into Meera’s mind. When a familiar texture or the sight of a police uniform now slips into her awareness, Meera’s thoughts spiral. She recalls, with a jolt, the crushing sensation of that officer’s hand, and instantly she believes she can’t cope with even the slightest upset. The texture of a rough carpet, the feel of a metal door handle, the sight of a uniform in the hallway—all act as sirens, reminding her that danger could still strike. Each time she confronts one of these triggers, she feels her stomach tighten, her breathing shallow, and her mind filled with the conviction that the world has become an arena where no good can happen. This immediate shift from comfort to alarm sets the stage for her pervasive negative appraisal of the world. Meera’s negative beliefs have seeped into the very way she remembers that night. She tells herself that if she were able to recall the event in a coherent way, she would be able to process it, yet the very act of trying feels impossible. Her memories are fragmented, arriving as disjointed flashes of an officer’s grip, a siren’s wail, a distant shout, each piece a ghost that refuses to fit together. Because she believes she has no coping resources, her brain guards the details, keeping them out of reach. The gaps in her recollection, the feeling that she cannot find the words to describe the assault, reinforce her belief that she is powerless and that nothing good can happen. The more she thinks she is unable to handle, the more her memories stay locked, as if the body itself is a weapon that refuses to let the past be known. These negative appraisals then fan the flames of the triggers that loom over her everyday life. Meera has learned that the mere presence of a police officer in a room can bring a wave of anxiety that feels like an immediate threat. The memory of being seized and the knowledge that she can’t cope even with minor discomfort make her hyper‑vigilant for any sign of authority. This vigilance makes her more sensitive to subtle cues—a badge in a camera frame, a uniformed figure in a news report—that she would once have dismissed. The more she anticipates danger, the more likely she is to over‑react to innocuous signals, perpetuating her belief that the world is hostile. Her fragmented recollection, in turn, fuels the triggers that she can no longer ignore. Each time she tries to speak about the assault, she feels a disjointed rush of images that overwhelm her ability to narrate. She can sense the texture of the officer’s gloves in her memory, but she cannot articulate the feeling. The memory’s incoherence makes the texture feel more present and more vivid, as if the body is still pressed against a rough surface. The sudden return of this sensory cue triggers a panic that brings the same physical symptoms she once felt on the night she was assaulted. Thus, the memory and the trigger feed one another in a self‑reinforcing loop, keeping her in a state of hyperarousal. In her work as an interior designer, Meera now avoids certain materials. She refuses to use rough-textured fabrics or concrete surfaces in client proposals, fearing that their feel will conjure the officer’s grip. She no longer participates in community meetings that involve police oversight, citing an “unmanageable anxiety” whenever she is asked to attend. The avoidance has cost her several high‑profile contracts, as clients expect modern, textured finishes that she cannot safely incorporate. Her social life has shrunk; she has withdrawn from the neighborhood association she once chaired, feeling that the presence of uniforms in any public space will spark a flashback. The decision to seek help came after her grandson, a volunteer firefighter, told her that she seemed “stuck in a nightmare.” Meera’s heart raced at the thought of being unable to control her reactions, and she feared that if she did not intervene, she would lose the last threads of the life she had built. She now hopes that understanding why these triggers, memories, and negative beliefs are linked will allow her to loosen the grip the past has on her present. The most frightening thought remains the certainty that her body will betray her again, that a texture or a uniform might feel like a looming threat, and that she will fail to keep herself safe.
